title: Object Storage
objectives: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Object stores are durable (11 nines), cheap and scale infinitely. Clients upload directly with pre-signed URLs; metadata goes to a DB; processing runs async.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Store blobs in S3-like object stores; upload via pre-signed URLs; serve via CDN.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client asks for upload URL” to “CDN serves”, via “Pre-signed URL”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Storing images as BLOBs in the relational DB.

questions.prompt: Why use pre-signed URLs for uploads?

choices.label: They compress the files before they reach storage
They replace authentication for the whole upload API
They make the uploaded files public to everyone forever
Clients upload straight to the bucket, so large files skip your app servers

questions.explanation: The app only signs; the bucket receives the bytes.

questions.prompt: 1M uploads a day at 2 MB each. Storage added per year, in TB?
questions.workedAnswer: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB a day; 2 TB × 365 = 730 TB.
questions.explanation: 1M × 2 MB = 2 TB a day; 2 TB × 365 = 730 TB.

questions.prompt: Why not store images as BLOBs in Postgres?

choices.label: Images would load faster from Postgres than from a bucket and CDN
It bloats the database, backups and replication; object storage is cheaper and built for it
Postgres cannot store binary data of any size in a column
BLOB columns cannot be backed up or replicated by Postgres at all

questions.explanation: Keep the database for metadata.

questions.prompt: Order a media upload.

items.label: Client asks for an upload URL
Client uploads directly to the bucket

questions.explanation: Processing is asynchronous.

questions.prompt: Where do a photo’s owner, caption and object key go?

choices.label: In the bucket’s name, one bucket per photo
In the CDN configuration for that path
Inside the image file’s metadata only
In a database row that points at the object

questions.explanation: Objects hold bytes; the database holds what you query.

flashcards.back: Metadata in DB, bytes in object store.

title: HDFS
objectives: Describe the NameNode/DataNode split
Explain block replication and rack awareness
Know where HDFS fits and where it does not

cards.title: Big files, big blocks
cards.body: HDFS stores huge files split into large blocks (128 MB by default) across many DataNodes. One NameNode keeps the metadata: which blocks make up a file and where they live.

cards.title: Replication
cards.body: Each block is stored three times by default, with copies on different racks so a rack power failure does not lose data. Lost replicas are re-copied automatically.

cards.title: Reading a file
cards.body: 4 steps from “Client asks NameNode for block locations” to “NameNode never touches the data”, via “NameNode returns DataNodes per block”.
steps: Client asks NameNode for block locations
Client streams blocks directly from DataNodes

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using HDFS for millions of tiny files or low-latency lookups. Each file costs NameNode memory, and HDFS is built for large sequential scans, not serving user requests.

questions.prompt: Why are HDFS replicas placed on different racks?

choices.label: Because two DataNodes cannot share a rack
To make writes faster across the cluster
To use less storage for each block copy
So one rack failure (power, switch) does not lose every copy

questions.explanation: Spread copies across failure domains.

questions.prompt: Which workload is a poor fit for HDFS?

choices.label: Scanning 50 TB of logs every night
Large Parquet files for Spark jobs
Millions of tiny files served to users with low latency
Archiving raw clickstream for batch jobs

questions.explanation: Every file costs NameNode memory, and HDFS is built for big scans.

questions.prompt: Order an HDFS read.

items.label: Client asks the NameNode for block locations
Data never passes through the NameNode

questions.explanation: The NameNode only handles metadata.

questions.prompt: What does the NameNode store?

choices.label: User passwords and access keys
Only the newest blocks of each file
Metadata: each file’s blocks and their locations
The file data itself, kept in RAM

questions.explanation: DataNodes store the blocks.

questions.prompt: A 1,024 MB file in 128 MB blocks with 3× replication. How many block replicas are stored?
questions.explanation: 1,024 MB ÷ 128 MB = 8 blocks; 8 × 3 = 24 replicas.

flashcards.back: Metadata: file to block mapping and block locations, not the data.
Three copies, spread across racks.
Large sequential batch reads, not tiny files or low-latency lookups.

title: Inverted Index & Elasticsearch
objectives: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: An inverted index maps terms → documents. Analysers tokenise, lowercase and stem. Keep the DB as source of truth and sync to the search cluster via CDC or events.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: Full-text search uses inverted indexes (Elasticsearch/OpenSearch) built from the primary DB.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 6 steps from “Write to DB” to “ranked results”, via “CDC event”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Using SQL LIKE "%term%" on millions of rows for search.

questions.prompt: Why not search with LIKE '%paneer%' on millions of rows?

choices.label: LIKE cannot match Hindi or other Unicode text
A leading wildcard cannot use an index, so every row is scanned
LIKE only matches text stored in uppercase
LIKE locks the whole table while it runs

questions.explanation: Inverted indexes find terms without scanning.

questions.prompt: An inverted index maps:

choices.label: Each user to their searches
Each document to its byte offset
Each document to its primary key
Each term to the documents that contain it

questions.explanation: Term → posting list.

questions.prompt: A search for “running” should match “run”. Which step does that?

choices.label: Adding a B-tree index
Stemming in the analyser
Adding replicas
Sharding the index

questions.explanation: Analysers tokenise, lowercase and stem.

questions.prompt: Order how a product reaches search results.
questions.explanation: The database is written first.

questions.prompt: After an outage, the search cluster and the database disagree. Which wins?

choices.label: The search cluster: it has the newer data
Whichever of the two was written last
The database: re-sync or rebuild the index from it
Neither: rebuild both from empty

questions.explanation: Search is a derived copy.

flashcards.back: Term → list of document IDs.
Primary DB; search index is derived.

title: MapReduce & Spark
objectives: Explain map, shuffle and reduce
Say why Spark beats MapReduce for multi-step jobs
Spot and fix skew in a shuffle

cards.title: MapReduce
cards.body: Map: each worker reads a chunk and emits key-value pairs, such as (word, 1). Shuffle: pairs with the same key go to the same reducer. Reduce: combine the values per key. Moving computation to the data beats moving data.

cards.title: Counting words
cards.body: 5 steps from “Split input into chunks” to “Write the results”, via “Map: emit (word, 1)”.

cards.title: Spark
cards.body: Spark keeps intermediate data in memory across steps instead of writing to disk after every MapReduce stage, so multi-step jobs and iterative ML run much faster. Lost partitions are recomputed from lineage.

cards.title: Shuffles are expensive
cards.body: The shuffle moves data across the network. A skewed key, such as one celebrity’s id, sends most data to one reducer, which runs for hours while the rest finish. Salt hot keys or pre-aggregate.

cards.title: Batch or stream?
cards.body: Batch jobs process a bounded dataset, such as yesterday’s orders, with high throughput and minutes-to-hours latency. Use streaming when decisions must happen in seconds.

questions.prompt: In a MapReduce word count, what happens in the shuffle?

choices.label: Each input line is split into separate words
The input files are compressed for transfer
Pairs with the same word are sent to the same reducer
The counts for each word are added together

questions.explanation: Grouping by key happens between map and reduce.

questions.prompt: Why is Spark faster than classic MapReduce for multi-step jobs?

choices.label: It runs the whole job on a single large machine
It keeps intermediate data in memory between steps
It never recomputes anything, even after a failure
It skips the shuffle step between map and reduce

questions.explanation: Disk round trips between stages dominate MapReduce.

questions.prompt: Order a word-count job.
questions.explanation: Map, shuffle, reduce.

questions.prompt: A nightly job groups views by creator. One creator has 40% of all views, and one reducer runs for hours. Click the bottleneck.
questions.explanation: Salt the hot key or pre-aggregate on the map side.

questions.prompt: Which fits a nightly batch job?

choices.label: Blocking a fraudulent card swipe
Recomputing yesterday’s seller payouts
Live match score updates
Surge pricing every 30 seconds

questions.explanation: Bounded data, hours of acceptable latency.

flashcards.front: In a MapReduce word count, what happens in the shuffle?
flashcards.back: Pairs with the same word are sent to the same reducer. Grouping by key happens between map and reduce.

flashcards.front: Why is Spark faster than classic MapReduce for multi-step jobs?
flashcards.back: It keeps intermediate data in memory instead of writing to disk between steps. Disk round trips between stages dominate MapReduce.

flashcards.front: Which fits a nightly batch job?
flashcards.back: Recomputing yesterday’s seller payouts. Bounded data, hours of acceptable latency.

title: Stream Processing
objectives: Contrast stream and batch processing
Explain windows and event time vs processing time
Handle late and duplicate events

cards.title: Results while data flows
cards.body: Batch jobs answer questions about yesterday. Stream processors (Flink, Kafka Streams, Spark Structured Streaming) update answers continuously, such as fraud scores within seconds of a UPI transaction.

cards.title: Windows
cards.body: Streams are unbounded, so you aggregate over windows: tumbling (fixed, non-overlapping), sliding (overlapping) or session (gaps of inactivity). Use event time, when it happened, not processing time, when it arrived.

cards.title: Counting clicks per minute
cards.body: 4 steps from “Clicks land in Kafka” to “Results written to a store for dashboards”, via “Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window”.
steps: Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window
Watermark decides when a window closes
Results written to a store for dashboards

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Assuming events arrive in order and exactly once. Mobile clients send late events and brokers redeliver, so use watermarks for lateness and idempotent or transactional sinks for duplicates.

questions.prompt: Phones go offline and upload clicks 10 minutes late. Which time should per-minute counts use?

choices.label: Processing time, because it is simpler
The broker’s append time
The time the server received the upload
Event time, with a watermark that allows late data

questions.explanation: Count clicks when they happened.

questions.prompt: Which fits stream processing rather than a nightly batch?

choices.label: Monthly GST reports
Recomputing yesterday’s payouts
Flagging a suspicious UPI transaction within seconds
Training a model on last year’s data

questions.explanation: Seconds matter only for the first.

questions.prompt: The broker redelivers messages after a consumer restart. What keeps counts correct?

choices.label: Idempotent or transactional writes to the sink
Ignore them: counts are approximate anyway
Use larger windows
Switch to processing time

questions.explanation: Redelivery is normal; the sink must absorb it.

questions.prompt: Order a clicks-per-minute pipeline.

items.label: Processor groups by ad and 1-minute event-time window
Watermark decides when a window closes
Results written to a store for dashboards

questions.explanation: The watermark trades lateness for latency.

questions.prompt: Count clicks per ad in non-overlapping 1-minute buckets. Which window?

choices.label: Sliding
A single global window
Session
Tumbling

questions.explanation: Fixed, non-overlapping.

flashcards.back: When the event happened vs when the system saw it.
Fixed-size, non-overlapping time buckets.
How long to wait for late events before closing a window.

title: Warehouse/Lake/OLAP
objectives: OLTP serves transactions; OLAP column stores serve aggregates over huge datasets.

cards.title: Why interviewers ask
cards.body: Row stores suit point reads/writes. Column stores (ClickHouse, BigQuery) compress columns and scan aggregates fast. Time-series DBs handle append-heavy metrics with downsampling.

cards.title: The core idea
cards.body: OLTP serves transactions; OLAP column stores serve aggregates over huge datasets.

cards.title: How a request flows
cards.body: 5 steps from “App writes OLTP” to “Dashboards”, via “CDC / ETL”.

cards.title: Watch out for
cards.body: Running heavy analytical queries on the production OLTP database.

questions.prompt: Best store for “average delivery time per city per hour over two years”?

choices.label: The search cluster, with an aggregation query
The production Postgres primary, with an index
Redis, with one sorted set per city
A columnar warehouse such as BigQuery or ClickHouse

questions.explanation: Large aggregates belong in OLAP.

questions.prompt: Why are column stores fast for “average price by city”?

choices.label: They read only the needed columns, which compress well
They index every column with a B-tree
They keep every row in memory
They avoid aggregation

questions.explanation: Fewer bytes scanned.

questions.prompt: Analysts run heavy reports on the production OLTP database. Risk?

choices.label: Long scans slow down checkout queries
Reports will be inaccurate
The database switches to read-only
Writes get lost

questions.explanation: Separate analytics from the transaction path.

questions.prompt: Order the path from app to dashboard.
questions.explanation: Analytics reads a copy.

questions.prompt: Which is an OLTP query?

choices.label: Top 100 products last quarter
Revenue by month over three years
Average delivery time per city
Insert one order and decrement its stock

questions.explanation: Small, transactional, row-level.

flashcards.back: Transactions vs analytics.
Reads only needed columns; high compression.

AWS Well-Architected Framework

title: Geospatial Indexing
objectives: Explain geohash and quadtree indexing
Answer “nearby” queries without scanning every row
Handle cell boundaries and dense cities

cards.title: Nearby without a full scan
cards.body: Computing distance to every restaurant in India per request is too slow. Geospatial indexes bucket locations into cells so a query only checks nearby cells.

cards.title: Geohash and quadtrees
cards.body: Geohash encodes lat/long into a string; a shared prefix means nearby. Quadtrees split space into four until each cell holds few points, so dense Mumbai gets small cells and rural areas get big ones.

cards.title: Finding restaurants within 2 km
cards.body: 4 steps from “Get user’s geohash cell” to “Compute exact distance and sort”, via “Add the 8 neighbouring cells”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Searching only the user’s own cell. A restaurant 50 m away can sit across a cell boundary, so always include neighbouring cells.

questions.prompt: A user stands at the edge of a geohash cell. Why also search the neighbouring cells?

choices.label: Geohash requires exactly 9 cells
A restaurant 50 m away can sit just across the boundary
Neighbouring cells are already cached
To balance load across shards

questions.explanation: Cells are arbitrary lines on the map.

questions.prompt: Why might a quadtree beat fixed-size grid cells for India?

choices.label: Quadtrees need no memory beyond the points themselves
Fixed grids cannot store latitude, only longitude
Quadtrees give exact road distances between places
Cells split where points are dense (small in Mumbai)

questions.explanation: Adaptive cells keep candidate counts even.

questions.prompt: Order a “nearby within 2 km” query.
questions.explanation: Coarse filter, then exact check.

questions.prompt: Two geohashes share a long prefix. What does that tell you?

choices.label: They are in the same country only
They are close together
One is north of the other
Nothing: prefixes are random

questions.explanation: A shared prefix means a shared cell.

questions.prompt: Index for “restaurants near me” across India.

rationaleOptions.label: Each query touches only a few cells
Scanning every restaurant is fine on fast CPUs

rationaleConflicts.r3: Computing distance to every restaurant per request is far too slow at this scale.

questions.explanation: Index space so queries stay local.

flashcards.front: What does a shared geohash prefix mean?
flashcards.back: The points are close (with edge cases at cell boundaries).

flashcards.front: Why do quadtrees suit uneven density?
flashcards.back: They split dense areas into smaller cells.
Nearby points can fall just across a cell boundary.

title: Time-Series DBs
objectives: Recognise time-series workloads
Explain downsampling and retention
Avoid high-cardinality labels

cards.title: Append-heavy, time-ordered
cards.body: Metrics, sensor readings and prices arrive as timestamped points, mostly appended and read as ranges (last hour, last week). Time-series databases compress and index for exactly that.

cards.title: Retention and rollups
cards.body: Raw 10-second points for 7 days, 1-minute averages for 90 days, hourly for years. Downsampling keeps dashboards fast and storage bounded.

cards.title: A metric’s life
cards.body: 5 steps from “Agent emits cpu{host=web-12}” to “Raw data expires after retention”, via “Ingest appends to the current time block”.
steps: Ingest appends to the current time block

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Putting user IDs or request IDs in labels. Every unique label combination is a new series, so cardinality explodes and memory with it.

questions.prompt: Metrics memory jumped 50× after a deploy that added a user_id label. Why?

choices.label: Compaction was turned off by the same deploy
user_id values are stored as long strings per sample
Each user id creates a new series, so the series count explodes
The database cannot index numeric label values

questions.explanation: Every label combination is a series.

questions.prompt: Dashboards over a year of 10-second data are slow and storage keeps growing. What helps most?

choices.label: Downsample older data and set retention
Move metrics into a relational database
Keep raw data forever on faster disks
Add more labels

questions.explanation: Rollups keep old data cheap to query.

questions.prompt: Which workload is most time-series shaped?

choices.label: A product catalogue
Orders with joins to customers
User profiles edited occasionally
CPU usage from 5,000 servers every 10 seconds

questions.explanation: Timestamped, append-heavy, read as ranges.

questions.prompt: Order a metric’s life.

items.label: Ingest appends it to the current block

questions.explanation: Raw data is short-lived; rollups last.

questions.prompt: 5,000 hosts each report 50 metrics every 10 s. How many points per second are ingested?
questions.workedAnswer: 5,000 × 50 = 250,000 series; one point per 10 s gives 25,000 points/s.
questions.explanation: 5,000 × 50 = 250,000 series; one point per 10 s gives 25,000 points/s.

flashcards.back: Replacing old raw points with coarser aggregates like 1-minute averages.
Unbounded label values such as user or request IDs.
A range scan over a time window for a series.

title: Blue-Green/Canary/Feature Flags
objectives: Compare blue-green and canary releases
Use feature flags and kill switches safely
Keep schema changes rollback-safe

cards.title: Blue-green
cards.body: Run two full environments. Deploy to the idle one (green), test it, then switch the router from blue to green. Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the switch, and database changes must work for both.

cards.title: Canary
cards.body: Send a small share of traffic (1%, then 5%, 25%) to the new version and watch error rates and latency. Roll back automatically if they get worse. It catches problems only real traffic shows.

cards.title: Feature flags
cards.body: Ship code dark and turn features on per user, region or percentage at runtime. Kill switches turn a broken feature off without a deploy. Remove flags once rolled out, or they pile up as untested paths.

cards.title: A canary rollout
cards.body: 5 steps from “Deploy v2 next to v1” to “Roll back if metrics worsen”, via “Route 1% of traffic to v2”.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Shipping a schema change the old version cannot read, then rolling back. Make changes backward compatible: add the new column, switch code, remove the old column later.

questions.prompt: What does a canary release do?

choices.label: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate
Tests only in staging
Switches all traffic at once and rolls back if users complain
Deploys to every server at 2 AM

questions.explanation: Real traffic, limited blast radius.

questions.prompt: In blue-green, how do you roll back?

choices.label: Redeploy the old build to every server
Wait for the next release
Restore the database from backup
Point the router back to the old environment

questions.explanation: The old environment is still running.

questions.prompt: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?

choices.label: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag
Hotfix and redeploy
Add servers
Roll back the whole release

questions.explanation: Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

questions.prompt: Order a canary rollout.
questions.explanation: Grow only while metrics hold.

questions.prompt: Order a rollback-safe column rename.

items.label: Switch reads to the new column

questions.explanation: Every step works with the previous code version.

flashcards.front: What does a canary release do?
flashcards.back: Sends a small share of traffic to v2 and compares its error rate. Real traffic, limited blast radius.

flashcards.front: In blue-green, how do you roll back?
flashcards.back: Point the router back to the old environment. The old environment is still running.

flashcards.front: A new recommendations widget is crashing the app. Fastest fix?
flashcards.back: Turn it off with its kill-switch flag. Flags change behaviour without a deploy.

title: Containers & Kubernetes
objectives: Explain what a container packages
Describe what Kubernetes schedules and heals
Use readiness vs liveness probes correctly

cards.title: Containers package the process
cards.body: A container image bundles your app and its dependencies, so it runs the same on a laptop and in production. It shares the host kernel, so it starts in seconds rather than minutes like a VM.

cards.title: Kubernetes runs the fleet
cards.body: You declare the desired state (5 replicas of checkout, 512 MB each). Kubernetes schedules pods onto nodes, restarts crashed ones and replaces pods when a node dies.

cards.title: A rolling deploy
cards.body: 5 steps from “New image pushed” to “One old pod is removed, repeat”, via “Deployment creates a new pod”.
steps: One old pod is removed, repeat

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using the liveness probe to check the database. If the DB blips, every pod fails liveness and gets restarted at once. Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: The database blips and every pod restarts in a loop. What is misconfigured?

choices.label: The image is too large
The readiness probe checks the database
The rolling update is too fast
The liveness probe checks the database

questions.explanation: Dependency checks belong in readiness, which only stops traffic.

questions.prompt: A node running three checkout pods dies. What does Kubernetes do?

choices.label: Schedules replacement pods on healthy nodes
Restarts the node
Waits for the node to come back
Moves traffic to another cluster

questions.explanation: Controllers restore the declared state.

questions.prompt: Order one step of a rolling deploy.
questions.explanation: Old pods leave only after new ones are ready.

questions.prompt: Why does a container start in seconds while a VM takes minutes?

choices.label: Containers skip the network stack entirely
Containers only run on bare-metal servers
It shares the host kernel instead of booting its own OS
Containers have no filesystem to mount

questions.explanation: No guest OS boot.

questions.prompt: You declared 5 replicas of checkout and one crashes. What happens?

choices.label: The whole Deployment is deleted and must be reapplied
Nothing happens until you run kubectl apply again
The other 4 pods restart to rebalance the traffic
Kubernetes sees 4 running instead of 5 and starts a new pod

questions.explanation: Reconciliation loops close the gap.

flashcards.back: Containers share the host kernel and start in seconds.
Failing it removes the pod from traffic without restarting it.
Failing it restarts the container.

title: Offset vs Cursor Pagination
objectives: Explain why deep offsets are slow
Implement cursor pagination with a stable key
Pick offset or cursor for a given screen

cards.title: Offset pagination
cards.body: LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000 is simple and lets users jump to page 500, but the database still walks past 10,000 rows, and inserts shift pages so items repeat or vanish.

cards.title: Cursor pagination
cards.body: Return an opaque cursor (the last item’s sort key) and fetch WHERE (created_at, id) < cursor LIMIT 20. Each page is an index seek, and new inserts do not shift what comes next. There is no jumping to page 500.

cards.title: Paging a feed with cursors
cards.body: 5 steps from “Client asks for the first 20” to “Repeat until there is no cursor”, via “Server returns items and next_cursor”.
steps: Server seeks past it using the index
Repeat until there is no cursor

cards.title: A stable sort key
cards.body: Cursors need a unique, ordered key. created_at alone can tie, so use (created_at, id), with an index on that pair.

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using OFFSET for an infinite feed. Deep pages get slower and new posts push items onto the next page, so users see duplicates.

questions.prompt: Why is OFFSET 100000 slow?

choices.label: The database still reads and discards 100,000 rows
The response contains 100,000 rows
It locks the table
OFFSET disables every index

questions.explanation: Offsets are skipped, not jumped over.

questions.prompt: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?

choices.label: The new posts appended at the bottom
Duplicates, as earlier items shift onto the next page
Nothing changes
An error

questions.explanation: Inserts move everything down.

questions.prompt: Which cursor key is safe?

choices.label: (created_at, id)
The page number
created_at alone
A random number

questions.explanation: Unique and ordered.

questions.prompt: Order cursor paging.
questions.explanation: Each page starts from the last one seen.

questions.prompt: Pagination for an admin table of 5,000 rows where staff jump to arbitrary pages.

rationaleOptions.label: Cursors let staff jump straight to page 37
Offset supports jumping to any page
At 5,000 rows the skipped rows cost little

rationaleConflicts.r3: Cursors only move forward from a known position.

questions.explanation: Small, stable tables with page jumps suit offsets.

flashcards.back: The database still reads and discards 100,000 rows. Offsets are skipped, not jumped over.

flashcards.front: A feed uses offset paging. New posts arrive while a user scrolls. What do they see?
flashcards.back: Duplicates, as earlier items shift onto the next page. Inserts move everything down.
(created_at, id). Unique and ordered.

title: Optimistic vs Pessimistic Locking
objectives: Contrast optimistic and pessimistic locking
Pick one based on contention
Implement version checks

cards.title: Two ways to stop lost updates
cards.body: Pessimistic locking takes a lock before reading (SELECT … FOR UPDATE), so others wait. Optimistic locking reads freely and checks a version at write time; if someone changed it, retry.

cards.title: Pick by contention
cards.body: Low contention (editing your own profile): optimistic, no waiting. High contention on one row (the last Tatkal seat): pessimistic or atomic updates, because optimistic retries would mostly fail.

cards.title: Optimistic update
cards.body: 4 steps from “Read row with version 7” to “0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry”, via “Compute new value”.
steps: 0 rows updated: someone else won, re-read and retry

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Holding a pessimistic lock while calling an external payment API. The lock lives for seconds and everything else queues behind it. Keep lock scopes short.

questions.prompt: Thousands race for the last 10 seats on one train at 10:00. Which approach suits the seat row?

choices.label: No locking, reconcile later
Pessimistic locking, or an atomic conditional update
Optimistic locking with retries
Read committed with no extra checks

questions.explanation: Under heavy contention, optimistic retries mostly fail.

questions.prompt: An optimistic UPDATE … WHERE version = 7 changes 0 rows. What happened?

choices.label: The transaction deadlocked with another one
The database deleted the row by mistake
The version column overflowed its type
Someone else updated it first; re-read and retry

questions.explanation: The version moved on.

questions.prompt: Users edit their own address now and then. Which approach fits?

choices.label: Optimistic locking
A distributed lock in Redis
Serializable isolation for every query
A pessimistic lock held for the whole edit form

questions.explanation: Low contention: no waiting needed.

questions.prompt: Order an optimistic update.

items.label: If 0 rows changed, re-read and retry

questions.explanation: Check at write time.

questions.prompt: Checkout locks the order row with SELECT … FOR UPDATE, then calls a payment API that takes 3 s. Other requests pile up. Click the cause.

title: OT vs CRDT
objectives: Explain why collaborative editing needs conflict resolution
Contrast OT and CRDTs
Know which needs a central server

cards.title: Concurrent edits collide
cards.body: Two people type into the same Google Doc paragraph at once. If each simply applies the other’s edit at the original position, their copies diverge.

cards.title: OT vs CRDT
cards.body: Operational Transformation rewrites incoming operations against concurrent ones, usually through a central server that orders them. CRDTs design data types whose merges always converge, so peers can sync in any order, even offline.

cards.title: Two users insert at once
cards.body: 4 steps from “A inserts “X” at position 5” to “Both copies converge”, via “B deletes position 2”.
steps: Server transforms A’s insert to position 4

cards.title: Common trap
cards.body: Using last-write-wins on whole documents. One user’s entire edit disappears. Merge at the operation or character level.

CRDTs
